title: Module 1: Introduction to Sonography and Physics

questions.stem: Ultrasound is best defined as sound with a frequency:
options: Below the range of human hearing
Above the range of human hearing
Within the range of human hearing
questions.explanation: Ultrasound is sound above the range of human hearing.
tags: Sound, Waves and Ultrasound Basics

questions.stem: Diagnostic ultrasound typically uses frequencies in the range of:
questions.explanation: Diagnostic ultrasound uses about 2–20 MHz.
tags: Sound, Waves and Ultrasound Basics

questions.stem: The human audible range is approximately:
questions.explanation: Humans hear about 20 Hz to 20 kHz.
tags: Sound, Waves and Ultrasound Basics

questions.stem: Sound with a frequency below 20 Hz is called:
questions.explanation: Infrasound is below 20 Hz.
tags: Sound, Waves and Ultrasound Basics

questions.stem: Sound is classified as which type of wave?
questions.explanation: Sound is a longitudinal mechanical wave.
tags: Sound, Waves and Ultrasound Basics

questions.stem: Which of the following requires a medium in order to travel?
questions.explanation: Sound is mechanical and needs a medium; the others are electromagnetic.
tags: Sound, Waves and Ultrasound Basics

questions.stem: Ultrasound cannot travel through:
questions.explanation: Ultrasound cannot travel through a vacuum.
tags: Sound, Waves and Ultrasound Basics

questions.stem: Unlike X-rays, diagnostic ultrasound is:
options: Able to travel through a vacuum
questions.explanation: Ultrasound is non-ionizing mechanical energy.
tags: Sound, Waves and Ultrasound Basics

questions.stem: A wave is best defined as:
options: A device that converts energy from one form to another
A repeating cycle of electrical signals
A mechanism that transfers energy from one location to another
questions.explanation: A wave transfers energy from one location to another.
tags: Sound, Waves and Ultrasound Basics

questions.stem: In a longitudinal wave, particle motion is:
options: Perpendicular to the direction of wave propagation
Along the direction of wave propagation
questions.explanation: Longitudinal motion is along the direction of propagation.
tags: Sound, Waves and Ultrasound Basics

questions.stem: Which wave has particle motion perpendicular to the direction of propagation?
questions.explanation: Transverse motion is perpendicular to propagation.
tags: Sound, Waves and Ultrasound Basics

questions.stem: In the word "sonography," the term "graphy" means:
questions.explanation: "Sono" means sound; "graphy" means to write or record.
tags: Sound, Waves and Ultrasound Basics

questions.stem: The sinking of the Titanic in 1912 increased demand for:
questions.explanation: The Titanic disaster drove demand for underwater detection.
tags: History of Ultrasound

questions.stem: SONAR stands for:
questions.explanation: SOund NAvigation And Ranging.
tags: History of Ultrasound

questions.stem: Diagnostic ultrasound was developed from:
questions.explanation: Diagnostic ultrasound grew out of SONAR.
tags: History of Ultrasound

questions.stem: In 1928, through-transmission ultrasound was used to:
questions.explanation: Sokolov used through-transmission for flaw detection in metals.
tags: History of Ultrasound

questions.stem: The first diagnostic finding with ultrasound (1949) was:
questions.explanation: Gallstones were the first diagnostic finding (1949).
tags: History of Ultrasound

questions.stem: A-mode and B-mode imaging were developed during the:
questions.explanation: A-mode and B-mode appeared in the 1950s–60s.
tags: History of Ultrasound

questions.stem: Gallstones were detectable because they:
options: Are less dense than surrounding tissue
Are denser than surrounding tissue, creating an impedance difference
questions.explanation: Gallstones are denser than surrounding tissue, giving an impedance difference.
tags: History of Ultrasound

questions.stem: A unique advantage of ultrasound is that it can assess:
options: Soft tissue structure and real-time blood flow without ionizing radiation
questions.explanation: Ultrasound shows soft tissue and blood flow without ionizing radiation.
tags: System Components, Transducer and Coupling Gel

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly describes the fundamental imaging chain?
options: Electrical signal → transducer → sound pulse → tissue interaction → echoes → transducer → electrical signal → image
Sound pulse → image → transducer → electrical signal
questions.explanation: Electrical signal → transducer → pulse → tissue → echoes → transducer → electrical signal → image.
tags: System Components, Transducer and Coupling Gel

questions.stem: An ultrasound image is constructed from:
options: Sound passing completely through the body, like an X-ray
questions.explanation: The image is built from the pattern of returning echoes.
tags: System Components, Transducer and Coupling Gel

questions.stem: The system console is used by the sonographer to adjust:
options: Gain, depth, frequency and Doppler settings
questions.explanation: The console adjusts gain, depth, frequency and Doppler.
tags: System Components, Transducer and Coupling Gel

questions.stem: The role of the transducer is to:
options: Generate ultrasound pulses and receive returning echoes
questions.explanation: The transducer transmits pulses and receives echoes.
tags: System Components, Transducer and Coupling Gel

questions.stem: During transmission, the transducer converts:
questions.explanation: On transmission, electrical energy becomes sound energy.
tags: System Components, Transducer and Coupling Gel

questions.stem: The main purpose of coupling gel is to:
options: Remove the air gap between the probe and skin
Increase the speed of sound in tissue
questions.explanation: Gel removes the air gap.
tags: System Components, Transducer and Coupling Gel

questions.stem: A tissue–air boundary reflects:
questions.explanation: A tissue–air boundary reflects almost all sound.
tags: System Components, Transducer and Coupling Gel

questions.stem: Which statement about coupling gel is correct?
options: It improves acoustic coupling between the transducer and the skin
It changes the frequency of the pulse
questions.explanation: Gel improves acoustic coupling; it does not make the image.
tags: System Components, Transducer and Coupling Gel

questions.stem: Which transducer is standard for adult cardiac sonography?
questions.explanation: Phased array is standard for adult echo.
tags: System Components, Transducer and Coupling Gel

questions.stem: Which transducer is commonly used for carotid and DVT studies?
questions.explanation: Linear probes are used for carotids and DVT studies.
tags: System Components, Transducer and Coupling Gel

questions.stem: Which transducer is commonly used for abdominal imaging and general OB?
questions.explanation: Curvilinear probes suit abdominal and general OB imaging.
tags: System Components, Transducer and Coupling Gel

questions.stem: An acoustic interface is:
questions.explanation: An acoustic interface is a boundary between two tissues.
tags: Acoustic Interfaces, Pulse-Echo and the Range Equation

questions.stem: Acoustic impedance depends on a tissue's:
options: Density and the speed of sound in it
questions.explanation: Impedance depends on density and speed of sound.
tags: Acoustic Interfaces, Pulse-Echo and the Range Equation

questions.stem: A greater acoustic impedance mismatch at an interface generally produces:
questions.explanation: Greater mismatch gives a stronger echo.
tags: Acoustic Interfaces, Pulse-Echo and the Range Equation

questions.stem: A very small impedance difference between adjacent tissues produces:
questions.explanation: A small difference gives a weak echo.
tags: Acoustic Interfaces, Pulse-Echo and the Range Equation

questions.stem: At an interface, the sound that is not reflected:
questions.explanation: Unreflected sound continues into deeper tissue.
tags: Acoustic Interfaces, Pulse-Echo and the Range Equation

questions.stem: In the pulse-echo technique, the pulse is very short so that the transducer spends most of its time:
questions.explanation: The pulse is short, so the transducer mostly listens.
tags: Acoustic Interfaces, Pulse-Echo and the Range Equation

questions.stem: The average speed of sound in soft tissue assumed by the system is:
questions.explanation: The system assumes 1540 m/s.
tags: Acoustic Interfaces, Pulse-Echo and the Range Equation

questions.stem: In the range equation, the result is divided by two because:
options: Sound speed is halved in tissue
Only half of the pulse returns
The pulse is two cycles long
Sound travels to the reflector and back (round trip)
questions.explanation: Sound travels to the reflector and back, so divide by two.
tags: Acoustic Interfaces, Pulse-Echo and the Range Equation

questions.stem: Echoes that return earlier are displayed:
questions.explanation: Earlier echoes are displayed nearer the transducer.
tags: Acoustic Interfaces, Pulse-Echo and the Range Equation

questions.stem: The accuracy of the range equation depends on:
options: The assumption that sound travels at 1540 m/s in soft tissue
questions.explanation: Range accuracy depends on the 1540 m/s assumption.
tags: Acoustic Interfaces, Pulse-Echo and the Range Equation

questions.stem: An echo returns 130 µs after the pulse is transmitted. Assuming c = 1540 m/s, the reflector depth is approximately:
tags: Acoustic Interfaces, Pulse-Echo and the Range Equation

questions.stem: A reflector is 5 cm deep. The round-trip time of the echo is approximately:
tags: Acoustic Interfaces, Pulse-Echo and the Range Equation

questions.stem: Echo from reflector X returns twice as late as the echo from reflector Y. Reflector X is:
options: Four times as deep as Y
questions.explanation: Twice the round-trip time means twice the depth.
tags: Acoustic Interfaces, Pulse-Echo and the Range Equation

questions.stem: Which is the first step of the pulse-echo technique?
options: The pulse interacts with tissue interfaces
The transducer generates a pulse of ultrasound
questions.explanation: The transducer generates the pulse first.
tags: Acoustic Interfaces, Pulse-Echo and the Range Equation

questions.stem: Echo ranging in SONAR is the same principle as:
questions.explanation: SONAR echo ranging is the pulse-echo principle.
tags: Acoustic Interfaces, Pulse-Echo and the Range Equation

questions.stem: Echo amplitude determines:
questions.explanation: Echo amplitude sets pixel brightness.
tags: Scan Lines, Brightness and Gray Scale

questions.stem: Echo travel time determines:
questions.explanation: Echo travel time sets display depth.
tags: Scan Lines, Brightness and Gray Scale

questions.stem: Echo information collected along one ultrasound beam forms:
questions.explanation: One beam gives one scan line.
tags: Scan Lines, Brightness and Gray Scale

questions.stem: In B-mode imaging, one pulse produces:
questions.explanation: One pulse equals one scan line.
tags: Scan Lines, Brightness and Gray Scale

questions.stem: A frame is:
options: A complete 2D image made from many scan lines
questions.explanation: A frame is a complete 2D image made of many scan lines.
tags: Scan Lines, Brightness and Gray Scale

questions.stem: A typical cross-sectional image is made of approximately how many scan lines?
questions.explanation: Typical images use about 96–256 scan lines (hundreds).
tags: Scan Lines, Brightness and Gray Scale

questions.stem: What happens when more scan lines are used to build each image frame?
options: Spatial sampling improves, but frame rate may decrease
questions.explanation: More lines improve spatial sampling but may lower frame rate.
tags: Scan Lines, Brightness and Gray Scale

questions.stem: A sufficiently high frame rate is especially important in cardiac imaging because:
questions.explanation: The heart moves rapidly, so frame rate matters.
tags: Scan Lines, Brightness and Gray Scale

questions.stem: A hyperechoic structure appears:
questions.explanation: Hyperechoic structures appear bright.
tags: Scan Lines, Brightness and Gray Scale

questions.stem: A hypoechoic area appears:
questions.explanation: Hypoechoic areas appear dark.
tags: Scan Lines, Brightness and Gray Scale

questions.stem: An anechoic structure:
options: Is the brightest on the image
Produces virtually no echoes and appears black
questions.explanation: Anechoic structures produce virtually no echoes and look black.
tags: Scan Lines, Brightness and Gray Scale

questions.stem: Which of the following typically appears bright because it is a strong reflector?
questions.explanation: The diaphragm is a strong reflector; the others are fluids.
tags: Scan Lines, Brightness and Gray Scale

questions.stem: Weak reflectors are typically:
questions.explanation: Fluid-filled structures are weak reflectors.
tags: Scan Lines, Brightness and Gray Scale

questions.stem: Blood normally appears dark in cardiac images because:
options: Red blood cells produce weak backscatter
questions.explanation: Red blood cells give weak backscatter; blood is not totally echo-free.
tags: Scan Lines, Brightness and Gray Scale

questions.stem: Different gray shades within tissue are caused by:
questions.explanation: Gray shades within tissue come from scattering.
tags: Scan Lines, Brightness and Gray Scale

questions.stem: An image that is too bright or too dark may reflect:
questions.explanation: Wrong brightness may reflect poor optimization such as gain.
tags: Scan Lines, Brightness and Gray Scale

questions.stem: Gray scale imaging is also known as:
questions.explanation: Gray scale imaging is B-mode.
tags: Scan Lines, Brightness and Gray Scale

questions.stem: Intermediate gray levels in the myocardium reveal:
questions.explanation: Intermediate gray levels reveal tissue texture.
tags: Scan Lines, Brightness and Gray Scale

questions.stem: A-mode displays echoes as:
options: Amplitude spikes along a depth axis
questions.explanation: A-mode shows amplitude spikes.
tags: Display Modes: A-, B- and M-mode

questions.stem: In A-mode, the position of each spike represents:
questions.explanation: Spike position shows depth.
tags: Display Modes: A-, B- and M-mode

questions.stem: A-mode is still used in:
questions.explanation: A-mode is used in ophthalmology and precise distance measurement.
tags: Display Modes: A-, B- and M-mode

questions.stem: In B-mode, the letter "B" stands for:
questions.explanation: B stands for brightness.
tags: Display Modes: A-, B- and M-mode

questions.stem: M-mode displays:
options: Motion along a single ultrasound beam over time
questions.explanation: M-mode shows motion along one beam over time.
tags: Display Modes: A-, B- and M-mode

questions.stem: On an M-mode display, the horizontal axis represents:
questions.explanation: The horizontal axis is time.
tags: Display Modes: A-, B- and M-mode

questions.stem: M-mode has very high temporal resolution because:
options: Only one beam line is sampled repeatedly
questions.explanation: One beam is sampled repeatedly, giving excellent temporal resolution.
tags: Display Modes: A-, B- and M-mode

questions.stem: Temporal resolution refers to:
options: The ability to separate two close objects side by side
How well ultrasound shows motion over time
questions.explanation: Temporal resolution is how well motion is shown over time.
tags: Display Modes: A-, B- and M-mode

questions.stem: In a linear scan format, the ultrasound beams are:
questions.explanation: Linear beams are parallel.
tags: Scan Formats: Linear, Sector and Curvilinear

questions.stem: A linear transducer produces an image that is:
questions.explanation: Linear images are rectangular.
tags: Scan Formats: Linear, Sector and Curvilinear

questions.stem: Linear transducers are commonly used for:
options: Superficial structures such as vessels, thyroid and breast
questions.explanation: Linear probes suit superficial structures.
tags: Scan Formats: Linear, Sector and Curvilinear

questions.stem: Linear transducers are not normally used for routine adult echocardiography because:
options: Their larger footprint does not fit between the ribs
questions.explanation: The large footprint does not fit between ribs.
tags: Scan Formats: Linear, Sector and Curvilinear

questions.stem: A sector (phased-array) image is produced by:
options: Electronically steering beams from a small footprint
Parallel beams starting at different elements
questions.explanation: Phased arrays steer beams electronically from a small footprint.
tags: Scan Formats: Linear, Sector and Curvilinear

questions.stem: The sector image has which typical shape?
questions.explanation: Sector images are fan-shaped.
tags: Scan Formats: Linear, Sector and Curvilinear

questions.stem: In a sector image, the field of view:
questions.explanation: The sector widens with depth.
tags: Scan Formats: Linear, Sector and Curvilinear

questions.stem: In a sector image, lateral resolution generally:
options: Improves only in the near field
Decreases with depth because scan lines spread apart
questions.explanation: Diverging scan lines reduce lateral resolution with depth.
tags: Scan Formats: Linear, Sector and Curvilinear

questions.stem: The curvilinear format is described as:
options: A combination of linear and sector characteristics
questions.explanation: Curvilinear combines linear and sector features.
tags: Scan Formats: Linear, Sector and Curvilinear

questions.stem: Curved-linear transducers are commonly used for:
questions.explanation: Used for abdominal, pelvic and obstetric imaging.
tags: Scan Formats: Linear, Sector and Curvilinear

questions.stem: A curved-linear array forms its image by:
options: Steering beams from a very small footprint
Activating groups of elements sequentially along its curved face
questions.explanation: Groups of elements fire sequentially along the curved face.
tags: Scan Formats: Linear, Sector and Curvilinear

questions.stem: A phased array differs from a curved-linear array in that it:
options: Electronically steers beams from a much smaller footprint
questions.explanation: A phased array steers from a much smaller footprint.
tags: Scan Formats: Linear, Sector and Curvilinear

questions.stem: Cardiac imaging typically uses frequencies of about:
questions.explanation: Cardiac imaging uses about 2–5 MHz.
tags: Scan Formats: Linear, Sector and Curvilinear

questions.stem: Why is the sector format well suited to cardiac imaging?
options: The heart lies behind ribs and lungs, and a small footprint fits between the ribs
questions.explanation: A small footprint fits between ribs; the heart lies behind ribs and lungs.
tags: Scan Formats: Linear, Sector and Curvilinear

questions.stem: Air in the lungs interferes with cardiac imaging because it:
options: Prevents effective transmission of the beam
questions.explanation: Lung air prevents effective beam transmission.
tags: Scan Formats: Linear, Sector and Curvilinear

questions.stem: Complete the memory aid: "Linear is straight, Sector spreads, Curvilinear …"
questions.explanation: Curvilinear combines the advantages of both.
tags: Scan Formats: Linear, Sector and Curvilinear

questions.stem: In a linear format, each scan line:
options: Begins at a different element position
Begins only at the centre of the transducer
questions.explanation: Each linear scan line starts at a different element position.
tags: Scan Formats: Linear, Sector and Curvilinear

questions.stem: A 2D ultrasound image displays:
questions.explanation: 2D shows one cross-sectional plane.
tags: 2D, 3D and Doppler

questions.stem: A 3D ultrasound dataset:
options: Is a volume that can be rotated and cropped to view from any angle
Is sampled along a single beam
questions.explanation: 3D is a volume that can be rotated and viewed from any angle.
tags: 2D, 3D and Doppler

questions.stem: 3D echocardiography is particularly useful for:
options: En-face views of the mitral valve and guiding structural procedures
questions.explanation: 3D gives en-face mitral valve views and guides structural procedures.
tags: 2D, 3D and Doppler

questions.stem: The relationship between 3D and 2D echocardiography is that 3D:
options: Supplements 2D when extra spatial information is needed
Is never used in cardiac imaging
Always has a higher frame rate than 2D
questions.explanation: 3D supplements, and does not replace, 2D.
tags: 2D, 3D and Doppler

questions.stem: The Doppler effect is:
options: Conversion of electrical energy to sound
A change in frequency of echoes returning from moving targets
A change in brightness with depth
questions.explanation: Doppler is a frequency shift from moving targets.
tags: 2D, 3D and Doppler

questions.stem: Echoes from red blood cells moving toward the transducer return with:
questions.explanation: Motion toward the transducer raises the echo frequency.
tags: 2D, 3D and Doppler

questions.stem: The Doppler frequency shift provides information about:
options: Direction and velocity of blood flow
questions.explanation: The shift gives direction and velocity of flow.
tags: 2D, 3D and Doppler

questions.stem: In medicine, Doppler is used to:
options: Monitor a baby's heart rate during delivery
questions.explanation: Doppler monitors a baby's heart rate during delivery.
tags: 2D, 3D and Doppler

questions.stem: Colour Doppler information is displayed superimposed on:
questions.explanation: Colour Doppler is overlaid on the B-mode image.
tags: 2D, 3D and Doppler

questions.stem: Differences in tissue stiffness and density create:
questions.explanation: Stiffness and density differences create interfaces.
tags: 2D, 3D and Doppler

questions.stem: Which statement best summarises how echoes form the image?
options: A greater impedance difference gives a stronger echo and a brighter dot
One pulse forms the entire image
Echo amplitude determines the depth of the dot
questions.explanation: Greater difference gives a stronger echo and a brighter dot.
tags: 2D, 3D and Doppler
